Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — accumulated profits
questions.question:
Assertion (A): On the retirement of a partner, General Reserve appearing in the balance sheet is credited to all the partners, including the retiring partner, in the old profit-sharing ratio.
Reason (R): The reserve was built up out of profits earned during the period when the retiring partner was a partner.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Accumulated profits and reserves are undistributed past profits. Because they were earned while the retiring partner was a partner (the Reason), he is entitled to his share, so they are distributed among ALL partners in the old ratio (the Assertion).
Why not the others: (B) The Reason directly explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Past profits (reserves, P&L credit balance) → all old partners, old ratio.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares at a premium
questions.question: 200 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called up, were forfeited after the holder had paid ₹4 per share. These shares were re-issued at ₹11 per share as fully paid. On completion of the re-issue, the amounts transferred to Capital Reserve and credited to Securities Premium are:
options: A) Capital Reserve ₹1,000; Securities Premium nil
D) Capital Reserve ₹800; Securities Premium nil
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Capital Reserve ₹800; Securities Premium ₹200
Step 1: Forfeited amount = 200 × ₹4 = ₹800 (Share Forfeiture A/c)
Step 2: Re-issue at ₹11 = face value ₹10 + premium ₹1, so there is no discount and nothing is debited to Share Forfeiture
Step 3: Premium = 200 × ₹1 = ₹200 → Securities Premium A/c
Step 4: The whole forfeited amount (₹800) is a capital profit → Capital Reserve
Common mistake: Adding the premium to Capital Reserve gives (A). Deducting the premium from the forfeited amount gives (C). Forgetting the premium gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Appropriation of profit when the firm incurs a loss
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. The deed provides interest on capital at 10% p.a. (capitals: A ₹2,00,000; B ₹1,00,000) and a salary of ₹12,000 p.a. to B, both as appropriations. During the year the firm suffered a loss of ₹30,000. The net amount debited to A for the year will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹18,000
Why: Interest on capital and salary are APPROPRIATIONS of profit. When there is a loss, there is nothing to appropriate, so neither is allowed. The loss is simply shared in the profit-sharing ratio.
Step 1: A's share of the loss = ₹30,000 × 3/5 = ₹18,000 (debit)
Common mistake: Allowing the appropriations first increases the loss to ₹72,000; A's 3/5 share of that is ₹43,200 (A), and netting his ₹20,000 interest against it gives ₹23,200 (B). Sharing the loss equally gives ₹15,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — half-yearly drawings
questions.question: Meena, a partner, withdrew ₹20,000 on 30 September 2025 and another ₹20,000 on 31 March 2026, the last day of the accounting year. Interest on drawings is charged at 12% p.a. The interest on her drawings is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,200
Given: Interest runs from the date of each drawing to 31 March 2026.
Step 1: ₹20,000 drawn on 30 September → 6 months: ₹20,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹1,200
Step 2: ₹20,000 drawn on 31 March → 0 months: nil
Step 3: Total interest = ₹1,200
Common mistake: Charging 6 months on both drawings gives ₹2,400 (A). Charging a full year on ₹40,000 gives ₹4,800 (C). Applying an average of 4.5 months to ₹40,000 gives ₹1,800 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Forfeiture of shares issued at a premium (premium received)
questions.question: Shares of ₹10 each were issued at a premium of ₹2, payable ₹3 on application, ₹5 on allotment (including the premium) and ₹4 on the first and final call. The holder of 100 shares paid the application and allotment money but not the call, and his shares were forfeited. The amount credited to the Share Forfeiture Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹600
Why: Share Forfeiture is credited only with the money received towards SHARE CAPITAL. The premium has been received, so it stays in Securities Premium.
Step 1: Capital received per share = ₹3 (application) + ₹3 (₹5 allotment − ₹2 premium) = ₹6
Step 2: Forfeiture = 100 × ₹6 = ₹600
Entry: Share Capital A/c Dr. ₹1,000; To Share First and Final Call A/c ₹400; To Share Forfeiture A/c ₹600
Common mistake: Including the premium gives ₹800 (A). ₹1,000 (B) is the called-up capital. ₹400 (D) is the unpaid call.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — sacrificing ratio when only one partner sacrifices
questions.question: A and B share profits equally. They admit C, and the new profit-sharing ratio of A, B and C is 3 : 2 : 1. The sacrificing ratio of A and B is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0 : 1 (only B sacrifices)
Step 1: A: 1/2 − 3/6 = 3/6 − 3/6 = 0 (no sacrifice)
Step 2: B: 1/2 − 2/6 = 3/6 − 2/6 = 1/6 (sacrifice)
Step 3: C's 1/6 share comes entirely from B → sacrificing ratio 0 : 1
Common mistake: Assuming equal sacrifice gives 1 : 1 (B). Using the new ratio of A and B gives 3 : 2 (C). Reversing the result gives (D).
Key point: Always compute the sacrifice partner by partner; never assume it.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Realisation profit with expenses paid by a partner
questions.question: On dissolution, assets other than cash with a book value of ₹1,50,000 realised ₹1,62,000. Creditors of ₹40,000 were paid in full. Realisation expenses of ₹2,000 were paid by partner A on behalf of the firm. The profit on realisation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹10,000
Step 1: Debit side = Assets ₹1,50,000 + Creditors paid ₹40,000 + Expenses paid by A ₹2,000 = ₹1,92,000
Step 2: Credit side = Creditors ₹40,000 + Cash from assets ₹1,62,000 = ₹2,02,000
Step 3: Profit = ₹10,000 (A's Capital A/c is also credited with the ₹2,000 he paid)
Common mistake: Ignoring the expenses gives ₹12,000 (A). Deducting the expenses twice gives ₹8,000 (B). Adding the expenses gives ₹14,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement and death — accounting treatment of items
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Item)
(A) Retiring partner's share of goodwill
(B) Amount due to a retiring partner that is not paid immediately
(C) Deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death
(D) Balance of the deceased partner's Capital Account

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Debited to the remaining partners in their gaining ratio
(II) Transferred to the retiring partner's Loan Account
(III) Debited to Profit and Loss Suspense Account
(IV) Transferred to his Executor's Account

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) The gaining partners compensate the retiring partner for the share they acquire → gaining ratio (I).
(B) An unpaid balance becomes a liability → retiring partner's Loan A/c (II).
(C) The deceased partner's profit share is estimated → P&L Suspense A/c Dr. (III).
(D) The deceased partner's dues are payable to his legal representative → Executor's A/c (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the goodwill and loan treatments; (C) swaps the loan and executor accounts; (D) swaps goodwill and P&L Suspense.
Key point: Retirement → Loan A/c; death → Executor's A/c.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — omitted salary and wrong rate of interest
questions.question: A and B share profits equally, and their fixed capitals are ₹2,00,000 and ₹1,00,000. After the accounts were closed, it was found that: (i) A's salary of ₹12,000 had been omitted; and (ii) interest on capital had been allowed at 12% p.a. instead of 10% p.a. The single adjusting entry will be:
options: A) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To B's Current A/c ₹5,000
B) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹6,000; To A's Current A/c ₹6,000
C) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To A's Current A/c ₹5,000
D) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹8,000; To A's Current A/c ₹8,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹5,000; To A's Current A/c ₹5,000
Step 1: Salary to be credited: A +₹12,000
Step 2: Excess interest to be reversed (2%): A −₹4,000; B −₹2,000
Step 3: Net change in appropriations = 12,000 − 6,000 = +₹6,000, so profit must be reduced by ₹6,000, shared equally: A −₹3,000; B −₹3,000
Step 4: Net effect: A = 12,000 − 4,000 − 3,000 = +₹5,000; B = −2,000 − 3,000 = −₹5,000
Common mistake: Reversing the entry gives (A). Using the net change in appropriations of ₹6,000 as the transfer gives (B). Ignoring the profit adjustment and A's interest reversal gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Accounts transferred to the Realisation Account
questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, which of the following is NOT transferred to the debit side of the Realisation Account?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cash in hand
Why: Cash and bank balances are the means of settlement. They stay in the Cash/Bank Account, which records all receipts from assets and all payments. Every other asset (stock, debtors, machinery and so on) is transferred to the debit of the Realisation Account at book value.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are non-cash assets that have to be realised.
Key point: Realisation A/c — all assets except cash, bank and fictitious assets.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution of a firm — modes
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the dissolution of a partnership firm under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932:
(A) A firm may be dissolved with the consent of all the partners.
(B) A firm is compulsorily dissolved when its business becomes unlawful.
(C) A firm may be dissolved by an order of the court.
(D) A firm is automatically dissolved whenever a new partner is admitted.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: The Act provides for dissolution by agreement (Section 40), compulsory dissolution, for example when the business becomes illegal (Section 41), on certain contingencies (Section 42), by notice in a partnership at will (Section 43), and by the court (Section 44).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — admitting a partner only RECONSTITUTES the firm (dissolution of the partnership), and the firm itself continues. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Reconstitution changes the partnership; dissolution ends the firm.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Fixed versus fluctuating capital — current accounts
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Partners' Current Accounts are maintained when the capitals of the partners are fluctuating.
Reason (R): Under the fluctuating capital method, all adjustments such as profit, interest and drawings are made in the partners' Capital Accounts.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: Under the fluctuating capital method there is only ONE account per partner — the Capital Account — and every adjustment goes there (the Reason is true). That is exactly why no Current Account is needed. Current Accounts are a feature of the FIXED capital method, so the Assertion is false.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) treat the Assertion as true.
Key point: Current Account ⇔ fixed capital method.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Calls in arrears
questions.question: A company made a first call of ₹3 per share on 1,000 equity shares. A shareholder holding 200 shares failed to pay the call. The company maintains a Calls in Arrears Account. The amount debited to the Calls in Arrears Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹600
Step 1: Unpaid = 200 shares × ₹3 = ₹600
Entry: Bank A/c Dr. ₹2,400; Calls in Arrears A/c Dr. ₹600; To Share First Call A/c ₹3,000
Common mistake: ₹3,000 (A) is the total call money due. ₹2,400 (B) is the amount actually received. ₹200 (C) is the number of shares, not an amount.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Admission — new partner unable to bring premium
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2. C is admitted for a 1/4th share, which he takes from A and B in their old ratio. The firm's goodwill is valued at ₹80,000, but C is unable to bring any premium for goodwill in cash. In the entry for goodwill, the amount credited to A's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹12,000
Given: C's share of goodwill = ₹80,000 × 1/4 = ₹20,000; since he takes his share in the old ratio, the sacrificing ratio = 3 : 2.
Step 1: Entry: C's Current A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To A's Capital A/c and To B's Capital A/c (in the sacrificing ratio)
Step 2: A's credit = ₹20,000 × 3/5 = ₹12,000 (B gets ₹8,000)
Common mistake: ₹20,000 (B) is C's total share. Sharing it equally gives ₹10,000 (C). ₹48,000 (D) is A's share of the whole goodwill, which is never raised under AS-26.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Presentation of debentures in the balance sheet
questions.question: As per Schedule III, the portion of debentures that is repayable within twelve months from the balance sheet date is shown under:
options: A) Other current liabilities (current maturities of long-term debt)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Other current liabilities (current maturities of long-term debt)
Why: Debentures are long-term borrowings, but the part that falls due within the next 12 months becomes a current obligation. Schedule III shows it as 'Current maturities of long-term debt' under Other current liabilities.
Why not the others:
(B) Only the portion due after 12 months stays under long-term borrowings.
(C) Provisions are for uncertain amounts.
(D) Trade payables arise from purchases of goods and services.
Key point: Due within 12 months → current, even if the debt was originally long-term.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares at a premium
questions.question: When a company issues shares at a premium, the amount of premium is credited to:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Securities Premium Account
Why: Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the premium on issue of securities to be transferred to a separate 'Securities Premium Account', which can be used only for the purposes specified in that Section.
Why not the others:
(A) Capital Reserve holds capital profits, such as the surplus on re-issue of forfeited shares.
(B) General Reserve is created out of revenue profits.
(D) Share Capital is credited only with the face value.
Key point: Face value → Share Capital; excess over face value → Securities Premium.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — hidden goodwill from payment in full settlement
questions.question: C, who has a 1/5th share of profits, retires. After all adjustments except goodwill, his Capital Account shows a balance of ₹55,000. The remaining partners pay him ₹70,000 in full settlement, and the excess is treated as his share of goodwill. The firm's goodwill implied by this payment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹75,000
Step 1: C's share of goodwill = Amount paid − Balance due = ₹70,000 − ₹55,000 = ₹15,000
Step 2: This is 1/5th of the firm's goodwill → firm's goodwill = ₹15,000 × 5 = ₹75,000
Step 3: Entry: the remaining partners' Capital A/cs Dr. ₹15,000 (gaining ratio); To C's Capital A/c ₹15,000
Common mistake: ₹15,000 (A) is C's share, not the firm's goodwill. Multiplying the whole payment by 5 gives ₹3,50,000 (B). ₹70,000 (C) is the settlement amount.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — occasions for valuation
questions.question: On which of the following occasions is valuation of goodwill NOT required?
options: A) Admission of a new partner
C) Change in the profit-sharing ratio of existing partners
D) Introduction of additional capital by an existing partner
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Introduction of additional capital by an existing partner
Why: Goodwill is valued whenever partners' rights to future profits change: admission, retirement, death, change in profit-sharing ratio, amalgamation or sale of the business. Bringing in extra capital does not change anyone's share of profits.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) each change the partners' shares in future profits, so whoever gains must compensate whoever loses through goodwill.
Key point: A change in profit shares means goodwill must be valued.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — drawings for part of the year
questions.question: A partner withdrew ₹3,000 in the middle of every month from July 2025 to March 2026 (9 drawings). The books are closed on 31 March 2026, and interest on drawings is charged at 10% p.a. The interest on drawings is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,012.50
Given: Total drawings = 9 × ₹3,000 = ₹27,000, each in the middle of the month.
Step 1: The first drawing (mid-July) earns interest for 8.5 months and the last (mid-March) for 0.5 month
Step 2: Average period = (8.5 + 0.5) ÷ 2 = 4.5 months
Step 3: Interest = ₹27,000 × 10% × 4.5/12 = ₹1,012.50
Common mistake: Using 6 months as if the drawings covered the whole year gives ₹1,350 (B). Charging a full year gives ₹2,700 (C). Using (9 + 1) ÷ 2 = 5 months gives ₹1,125 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Settlement of a partner's debit balance
questions.question: On dissolution, after all adjustments, partner B's Capital Account shows a DEBIT balance of ₹8,000. B is solvent. The correct treatment is:
options: A) It is written off against the other partners' capitals
B) B brings ₹8,000 in cash to settle his account
C) It is transferred to the Realisation Account
D) It is ignored, as the firm is closing down
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B brings ₹8,000 in cash to settle his account
Why: A debit balance means B owes the firm. A solvent partner must pay it: Cash A/c Dr. ₹8,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹8,000. That money is then used to pay the partners who have credit balances.
Why not the others:
(A) The other partners bear such a deficiency only in insolvency, which is outside this syllabus.
(C) The Realisation Account is already closed by this stage.
(D) The partners' accounts must all be settled before the firm closes.
Key point: Debit balance → partner brings cash; credit balance → partner is paid cash.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — average profit with abnormal items
questions.question: A firm's profits were: 2022-23 ₹1,00,000; 2023-24 ₹1,20,000 (including an abnormal gain of ₹20,000); and 2024-25 ₹90,000 (after charging an abnormal loss of ₹15,000). Goodwill is to be valued at three years' purchase of the average NORMAL profit. The value of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹3,05,000
Why: Abnormal items will not recur, so they are removed — deduct abnormal gains and add back abnormal losses.
Step 1: Normal profits: 2022-23 ₹1,00,000; 2023-24 ₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,00,000; 2024-25 ₹90,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹1,05,000
Step 2: Average = ₹3,05,000 ÷ 3 = ₹1,01,667
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹1,01,667 × 3 = ₹3,05,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the abnormal items gives ₹3,10,000 (A). Deducting the abnormal loss instead of adding it back gives ₹2,75,000 (B). ₹1,01,667 (D) is the average profit before multiplying.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Nature of partnership — features
questions.question:
Which of the following are essential features of a partnership?
(A) An agreement between two or more persons
(B) A business carried on with a profit motive
(C) The business is carried on by all the partners or any of them acting for all (mutual agency)
(D) The liability of partners is limited to their capital contribution
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed (A) to share the profits of a business (B) carried on by all or any of them acting for all (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — partners of an ordinary firm have UNLIMITED liability, and their personal assets can be used to pay the firm's debts. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Agreement + business + profit sharing + mutual agency; unlimited liability.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Nature of partnership firm — governing law
questions.question: Partnership firms in India are governed by the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Indian Partnership Act, 1932
Why: Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 defines partnership, and the Act lays down the rights, duties and liabilities of partners, including the rules that apply when there is no deed (Section 13).
Why not the others:
(A) The Companies Act governs companies.
(B) The Contract Act governs contracts in general; partnership has its own Act.
(C) The LLP Act governs limited liability partnerships, which are a different form of business.
Key point: Ordinary partnership → Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — super profit after partners' remuneration
questions.question: A firm's average profit BEFORE partners' remuneration is ₹1,20,000. A reasonable remuneration of ₹20,000 p.a. for the partners' services is to be deducted. Capital employed is ₹8,00,000 and the normal rate of return is 10%. Goodwill is valued at four years' purchase of super profit. Its value is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹80,000
Why: Average profit must be comparable with the normal return earned by others, so the cost of the partners' own services is deducted first.
Step 1: Adjusted average profit = ₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Normal profit = 10% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹80,000
Step 3: Super profit = ₹1,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹20,000
Step 4: Goodwill = ₹20,000 × 4 = ₹80,000
Common mistake: Not deducting the remuneration gives a super profit of ₹40,000 and goodwill of ₹1,60,000 (A). ₹20,000 (C) is the super profit only. Multiplying the adjusted average profit by 4 gives ₹4,00,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital treated as a charge
questions.question: A and B share profits equally and their capitals are ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. Their deed says that interest on capital at 10% p.a. is to be allowed as a CHARGE, even if the firm suffers a loss. The profit before interest on capital is ₹40,000. The net amount credited to A for the year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹25,000
Why: When interest on capital is a charge, it is allowed in full even if it turns the profit into a loss.
Step 1: Interest: A ₹30,000; B ₹20,000; total ₹50,000
Step 2: Result after interest = ₹40,000 − ₹50,000 = loss of ₹10,000, shared equally: A −₹5,000; B −₹5,000
Step 3: A's net credit = ₹30,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹25,000
Common mistake: Treating interest as an appropriation (profit shared in the ratio of interest) gives ₹24,000 (A). Ignoring the resulting loss gives ₹30,000 (C). Sharing the ₹40,000 profit equally gives ₹20,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death — share of profit based on average profit
questions.question: R, a partner with a 1/3rd share of profits, died on 31 August 2025. The firm closes its books on 31 March. The deed provides that his share of profit up to the date of death is to be based on the average profit of the last three years, which was ₹1,20,000. R's share of profit up to the date of death is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹16,667
Given: 1 April to 31 August 2025 = 5 months; average profit ₹1,20,000; R's share 1/3.
Step 1: Profit for 5 months = ₹1,20,000 × 5/12 = ₹50,000
Step 2: R's share = ₹50,000 × 1/3 = ₹16,667 (approx.), debited to Profit and Loss Suspense A/c
Common mistake: Taking R's share for a full year gives ₹40,000 (A). Counting 4 months gives ₹13,333 (B). ₹50,000 (D) is the firm's profit for the period, not R's share.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Presentation of share capital — forfeiture and reserves
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II with reference to a company's balance sheet as per Schedule III:

List-I (Item)
(A) Share Forfeiture Account (shares not yet re-issued)
(B) Capital Reserve arising on re-issue of forfeited shares
(C) Securities Premium
(D) Calls in arrears

List-II (Presentation)
(I) Reserves and Surplus, shown as Capital Reserve
(II) Reserves and Surplus, shown as Securities Premium
(III) Deducted from subscribed capital in the Share Capital note
(IV) Added to paid-up capital in the Share Capital note

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why:
(A) Until the shares are re-issued, the forfeited amount is shown as an addition to paid-up capital → (IV).
(B) The surplus on re-issued shares is a capital profit → Capital Reserve (I).
(C) Securities Premium is shown separately under Reserves and Surplus → (II).
(D) Calls in arrears reduce subscribed capital → (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the forfeiture and calls-in-arrears treatments; (B) swaps the two reserves; (C) puts the forfeiture balance under Reserves.
Key point: Forfeiture balance → Share Capital note; transferred surplus → Capital Reserve.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of forfeited shares — rules
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the re-issue of forfeited shares:
(A) Forfeited shares may be re-issued at a discount not exceeding the amount forfeited on those shares.
(B) The surplus on the shares re-issued is transferred to Capital Reserve.
(C) The discount allowed on re-issue is debited to the Share Forfeiture Account.
(D) Forfeited shares must be re-issued only at par.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — the discount on re-issue is limited to the amount forfeited.
(B) True — the balance relating to the re-issued shares is a capital profit.
(C) True — the discount is met out of the Share Forfeiture Account.
(D) False — forfeited shares may be re-issued at par, at a premium or at a discount.
Why not the others: Options (A), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Maximum discount on re-issue = amount forfeited on those shares.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — kinds
questions.question: Under the Companies Act, 2013, the share capital of a company limited by shares can be of two kinds, namely:
options: A) Equity capital and debenture capital
B) Equity share capital and preference share capital
C) Authorised capital and borrowed capital
D) Fixed capital and fluctuating capital
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Equity share capital and preference share capital
Why: Section 43 of the Companies Act, 2013 says share capital is of two kinds — equity (with or without differential rights) and preference.
Why not the others:
(A) and (C) Debentures and borrowings are debt, not share capital.
(D) Fixed and fluctuating capital are methods used for partnership capital accounts.
Key point: Shares = owners' capital (equity or preference); debentures = borrowed capital.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of debentures at a premium — instalments
questions.question: A company issued 5,000, 12% debentures of ₹100 each at a premium of 5%, payable ₹40 on application and ₹65 on allotment (including the premium). The amount credited to the 12% Debentures Account on allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹3,00,000
Step 1: Allotment money ₹65 per debenture = ₹60 towards face value + ₹5 premium
Step 2: Debentures credit = 5,000 × ₹60 = ₹3,00,000; Securities Premium credit = 5,000 × ₹5 = ₹25,000
Entry: Debenture Allotment A/c Dr. ₹3,25,000; To 12% Debentures A/c ₹3,00,000; To Securities Premium A/c ₹25,000
Common mistake: Crediting the whole allotment money gives ₹3,25,000 (B). ₹2,00,000 (C) is the application money. ₹25,000 (D) is the premium.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Securities Premium on forfeiture and re-issue
questions.question: A company issued 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2, with the premium payable along with the allotment money. The holder of 200 shares failed to pay the allotment and call money, and his shares were forfeited. These shares were later re-issued at ₹12 per share as fully paid. The balance in the Securities Premium Account after the re-issue is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹20,000
Step 1: On allotment, Securities Premium is credited on all shares = 10,000 × ₹2 = ₹20,000
Step 2: On forfeiture, the premium was NOT received on 200 shares → Securities Premium A/c Dr. 200 × ₹2 = ₹400 (balance ₹19,600)
Step 3: On re-issue at ₹12 (premium ₹2) → Securities Premium A/c Cr. ₹400
Step 4: Final balance = ₹19,600 + ₹400 = ₹20,000
Common mistake: Stopping after the forfeiture gives ₹19,600 (A). Forgetting the forfeiture reversal gives ₹20,400 (C). ₹400 (D) is only the premium on the re-issue.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Cash available for partners' capitals
questions.question: On dissolution, the firm had a cash balance of ₹20,000. Its assets realised ₹1,40,000. It paid creditors ₹60,000, realisation expenses ₹2,000, and partners' loans of ₹10,000. The total amount available for payment to the partners on their capital accounts is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹88,000
Why: Under Section 48, cash is used first for outside liabilities and expenses, then for partners' loans, and only the remainder goes towards capital.
Step 1: Total cash = Opening ₹20,000 + Realisation ₹1,40,000 = ₹1,60,000
Step 2: Less creditors ₹60,000, expenses ₹2,000 and partners' loans ₹10,000 = ₹72,000
Step 3: Available for capitals = ₹1,60,000 − ₹72,000 = ₹88,000
Common mistake: Forgetting the partners' loans gives ₹98,000 (A). Ignoring the opening cash gives ₹68,000 (B). ₹1,60,000 (D) is the total cash before any payments.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Cash received on a call — calls in advance and in arrears
questions.question: A company made the first and final call of ₹3 per share on 20,000 equity shares. A shareholder holding 400 shares had already paid this call in advance along with the allotment money, and another shareholder holding 600 shares failed to pay the call. The cash actually received on the call is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹57,000
Step 1: Total call due = 20,000 × ₹3 = ₹60,000
Step 2: Less calls already received in advance = 400 × ₹3 = ₹1,200 (adjusted: Calls in Advance A/c Dr.)
Step 3: Less calls in arrears = 600 × ₹3 = ₹1,800
Step 4: Cash received = ₹60,000 − ₹1,200 − ₹1,800 = ₹57,000
Common mistake: ₹60,000 (A) is the total due. Ignoring the advance gives ₹58,200 (B). Ignoring the arrears gives ₹58,800 (C).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Features of a company
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a company:
(A) It is a separate legal entity, distinct from its members.
(B) It enjoys perpetual succession.
(C) In a company limited by shares, a member's liability is limited to the amount unpaid on his shares.
(D) Members are personally liable for all the debts of the company.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: A company is an artificial person created by law. It can own property and sue in its own name (A). Its existence is not affected by members joining or leaving (B). Members' liability is limited to the unpaid amount on their shares (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — limited liability means members are NOT personally liable beyond the unpaid amount on their shares. Options (A), (B) and (D) all include (D).
Key point: Separate entity + perpetual succession + limited liability.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares — stages
questions.question:
Arrange the following stages in the issue of shares by a public company in the correct order:
(A) Issue of prospectus inviting the public to apply
(B) Receipt of applications along with application money
(C) Allotment of shares
(D) Making calls on the shares
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B), (C), (D)
Why: A public company first issues a prospectus (A). The public then applies with application money (B). After the minimum subscription is received, the directors allot the shares (C). The remaining money is collected later through calls (D).
Why not the others: (B) and (D) receive applications before the prospectus is issued; (C) allots before applications are received.
Key point: Prospectus → application → allotment → calls.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — gaining ratio
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

X, Y and Z share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. Z retires on 31 March 2026. On that date their books show: Capitals — X ₹2,00,000, Y ₹1,50,000 and Z ₹1,00,000; General Reserve ₹50,000; Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹12,000; Investments (book value) ₹80,000; and Machinery ₹1,60,000. It was agreed that: (i) the firm's goodwill be valued at ₹1,50,000; (ii) machinery be depreciated by 10%; (iii) investments be brought down to their market value of ₹74,000; (iv) X and Y will share future profits in the ratio 3 : 2; and (v) Z be paid ₹50,000 immediately, with the balance transferred to his Loan Account.

Question: The gaining ratio of X and Y is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1 : 1
Step 1: X's gain = 3/5 − 5/10 = 6/10 − 5/10 = 1/10
Step 2: Y's gain = 2/5 − 3/10 = 4/10 − 3/10 = 1/10
Step 3: Gaining ratio = 1 : 1
Common mistake: Taking the new ratio as the gaining ratio gives 3 : 2 (A). 5 : 3 (B) is the old ratio of X and Y. 2 : 1 (C) has no basis in the data.
Key point: Gaining ratio = new share − old share, for each continuing partner.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — Investment Fluctuation Reserve
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

X, Y and Z share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. Z retires on 31 March 2026. On that date their books show: Capitals — X ₹2,00,000, Y ₹1,50,000 and Z ₹1,00,000; General Reserve ₹50,000; Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹12,000; Investments (book value) ₹80,000; and Machinery ₹1,60,000. It was agreed that: (i) the firm's goodwill be valued at ₹1,50,000; (ii) machinery be depreciated by 10%; (iii) investments be brought down to their market value of ₹74,000; (iv) X and Y will share future profits in the ratio 3 : 2; and (v) Z be paid ₹50,000 immediately, with the balance transferred to his Loan Account.

Question: Z's share of the balance of Investment Fluctuation Reserve (after meeting the fall in the value of investments) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,200
Why: The Investment Fluctuation Reserve exists to absorb a fall in the value of investments. The fall is met from the reserve first, and only the balance is distributed in the old ratio.
Step 1: Fall in value = ₹80,000 − ₹74,000 = ₹6,000 → Investment Fluctuation Reserve A/c Dr. ₹6,000; To Investments A/c ₹6,000
Step 2: Balance of reserve = ₹12,000 − ₹6,000 = ₹6,000
Step 3: Z's share = ₹6,000 × 2/10 = ₹1,200
Common mistake: Distributing the whole ₹12,000 gives Z ₹2,400 (B). Sharing equally among the three partners gives ₹2,000 (C). ₹6,000 (D) is the whole balance.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — retiring partner's share of goodwill
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

X, Y and Z share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. Z retires on 31 March 2026. On that date their books show: Capitals — X ₹2,00,000, Y ₹1,50,000 and Z ₹1,00,000; General Reserve ₹50,000; Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹12,000; Investments (book value) ₹80,000; and Machinery ₹1,60,000. It was agreed that: (i) the firm's goodwill be valued at ₹1,50,000; (ii) machinery be depreciated by 10%; (iii) investments be brought down to their market value of ₹74,000; (iv) X and Y will share future profits in the ratio 3 : 2; and (v) Z be paid ₹50,000 immediately, with the balance transferred to his Loan Account.

Question: Z's share of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹30,000
Step 1: Z's share = ₹1,50,000 × 2/10 = ₹30,000 (credited to Z's Capital A/c and debited to X and Y in their gaining ratio)
Common mistake: ₹1,50,000 (A) is the firm's goodwill. ₹15,000 (C) is each gaining partner's contribution. Taking a one-third share gives ₹50,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — amount transferred to Loan Account
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

X, Y and Z share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. Z retires on 31 March 2026. On that date their books show: Capitals — X ₹2,00,000, Y ₹1,50,000 and Z ₹1,00,000; General Reserve ₹50,000; Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹12,000; Investments (book value) ₹80,000; and Machinery ₹1,60,000. It was agreed that: (i) the firm's goodwill be valued at ₹1,50,000; (ii) machinery be depreciated by 10%; (iii) investments be brought down to their market value of ₹74,000; (iv) X and Y will share future profits in the ratio 3 : 2; and (v) Z be paid ₹50,000 immediately, with the balance transferred to his Loan Account.

Question: The amount transferred to Z's Loan Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹88,000
Step 1: Capital = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: General Reserve share = ₹50,000 × 2/10 = +₹10,000
Step 3: Investment Fluctuation Reserve balance share = +₹1,200
Step 4: Goodwill = +₹30,000
Step 5: Revaluation loss on machinery (10% of ₹1,60,000 = ₹16,000) × 2/10 = −₹3,200 (the fall in investments is met from the reserve, not the Revaluation A/c)
Step 6: Amount due = 1,00,000 + 10,000 + 1,200 + 30,000 − 3,200 = ₹1,38,000; less cash paid ₹50,000 = ₹88,000
Common mistake: ₹1,38,000 (A) is before the cash payment. Ignoring the machinery loss gives ₹91,200 (B). Ignoring the reserve balance gives ₹86,800 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — adjustment of goodwill
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

X, Y and Z share profits in the ratio 5 : 3 : 2. Z retires on 31 March 2026. On that date their books show: Capitals — X ₹2,00,000, Y ₹1,50,000 and Z ₹1,00,000; General Reserve ₹50,000; Investment Fluctuation Reserve ₹12,000; Investments (book value) ₹80,000; and Machinery ₹1,60,000. It was agreed that: (i) the firm's goodwill be valued at ₹1,50,000; (ii) machinery be depreciated by 10%; (iii) investments be brought down to their market value of ₹74,000; (iv) X and Y will share future profits in the ratio 3 : 2; and (v) Z be paid ₹50,000 immediately, with the balance transferred to his Loan Account.

Question: In the entry for Z's share of goodwill, the amount debited to Y's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹15,000
Given: Z's share of goodwill ₹30,000; gaining ratio of X and Y = 1 : 1.
Step 1: Y's share = ₹30,000 × 1/2 = ₹15,000
Entry: X's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; Y's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To Z's Capital A/c ₹30,000
Common mistake: Using the new ratio 3 : 2 gives Y ₹12,000 (A). Using the old ratio of X and Y (5 : 3) gives ₹11,250 (B). ₹30,000 (C) is Z's whole share.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Solvency ratios — total assets to debt ratio
questions.question: A company's total assets are ₹12,00,000 and its long-term debts are ₹4,00,000. Its total assets to debt ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3 : 1
Formula: Total assets to debt ratio = Total assets ÷ Long-term debts
Step 1: ₹12,00,000 ÷ ₹4,00,000 = 3 : 1 (each rupee of long-term debt is backed by ₹3 of assets)
Common mistake: Inverting the ratio gives 0.33 : 1 (A). Deducting the debt from total assets first gives 2 : 1 (B). Debt ÷ (assets − debt) gives 0.5 : 1 (C).
Key point: A higher ratio means better security for lenders.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Comparative statement of profit and loss
questions.question: In a comparative statement of profit and loss: revenue from operations increased from ₹4,00,000 in 2024-25 to ₹5,00,000 in 2025-26, and cost of revenue from operations increased from ₹2,40,000 to ₹3,15,000. The percentage change in gross profit is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 15.63%
Step 1: Gross profit 2024-25 = 4,00,000 − 2,40,000 = ₹1,60,000
Step 2: Gross profit 2025-26 = 5,00,000 − 3,15,000 = ₹1,85,000
Step 3: Change = ₹25,000; percentage change = 25,000 ÷ 1,60,000 × 100 = 15.63% (on the PREVIOUS year as base)
Common mistake: 25% (A) is the change in revenue. 31.25% (C) is the change in cost. Using the current year as the base gives 13.51% (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Activity ratios — finding closing inventory
questions.question: Cost of revenue from operations is ₹5,00,000 and the inventory turnover ratio is 5 times. If the opening inventory is ₹90,000, the closing inventory is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,10,000
Step 1: Average inventory = Cost of revenue ÷ Turnover = ₹5,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹1,00,000
Step 2: Average = (Opening + Closing) ÷ 2 → Opening + Closing = ₹2,00,000
Step 3: Closing = ₹2,00,000 − ₹90,000 = ₹1,10,000
Common mistake: ₹1,00,000 (B) is the average inventory. ₹90,000 (C) is the opening figure. ₹1,20,000 (D) comes from an arithmetic slip.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Profitability ratios — gross profit ratio (working back to purchases)
questions.question: A firm's gross profit ratio is 25% and its revenue from operations is ₹8,00,000. Opening inventory was ₹1,20,000 and closing inventory ₹80,000. Its purchases for the year were:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹5,60,000
Step 1: Gross profit = 25% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹2,00,000 → Cost of revenue = ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Cost of revenue = Opening inventory + Purchases − Closing inventory
Step 3: ₹6,00,000 = ₹1,20,000 + Purchases − ₹80,000 → Purchases = ₹5,60,000
Common mistake: Adding the opening inventory instead of deducting it gives ₹6,40,000 (A). ₹6,00,000 (B) is the cost of revenue. Taking 60% of revenue gives ₹4,80,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — finance and non-finance companies
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about the classification of cash flows as per AS-3 (Revised):
(A) For a finance company, interest received on loans given is an operating activity.
(B) For a non-finance company, dividend paid is a financing activity.
(C) Purchase of goodwill is an investing activity.
(D) For a non-finance company, proceeds from the sale of investments are an operating activity.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — lending is the main business of a finance company, so the interest it earns is operating.
(B) True — dividend is a return paid to the owners → financing.
(C) True — goodwill is a long-term (intangible) asset → investing.
(D) False — selling investments is an investing activity for a non-finance company.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Classification depends on the nature of the business — interest and dividend RECEIVED are operating for a finance company but investing for others.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — major heads
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major head on the 'Equity and Liabilities' side of a company's balance sheet as per Schedule III?
options: C) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets
Why: The Equity and Liabilities side has three major heads (in companies with share application money pending allotment, four): Shareholders' funds, Non-current liabilities and Current liabilities. Property, Plant and Equipment is a sub-head under Non-current ASSETS.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are the major heads of Equity and Liabilities.
Key point: Assets side — Non-current assets, Current assets; liabilities side — Shareholders' funds, Non-current liabilities, Current liabilities.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Solvency ratios — debt-equity ratio (working back)
questions.question: A company's debt-equity ratio is 0.5 : 1 and its long-term debts are ₹3,00,000. Its shareholders' funds are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹6,00,000
Formula: Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debts ÷ Shareholders' funds
Step 1: 0.5 = ₹3,00,000 ÷ Shareholders' funds → Shareholders' funds = ₹3,00,000 ÷ 0.5 = ₹6,00,000
Common mistake: Multiplying by 0.5 instead of dividing gives ₹1,50,000 (A). Assuming a 1 : 1 ratio gives ₹3,00,000 (C). ₹9,00,000 (D) is debt plus equity (total long-term funds).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — full computation
questions.question: From the following, calculate the net cash flow from operating activities: Net profit before tax ₹2,50,000; Depreciation ₹40,000; Goodwill written off ₹10,000; Increase in inventory ₹30,000; Decrease in trade receivables ₹20,000; Decrease in trade payables ₹15,000; Income tax paid ₹60,000.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹2,15,000
Step 1: Add back non-cash charges: 2,50,000 + 40,000 + 10,000 = ₹3,00,000
Step 2: Working-capital changes: inventory up −₹30,000; receivables down +₹20,000; payables down −₹15,000 → ₹2,75,000 (cash generated from operations)
Step 3: Less income tax paid ₹60,000 → net cash from operating activities = ₹2,15,000
Common mistake: Stopping before tax gives ₹2,75,000 (B). Deducting the fall in receivables instead of adding it gives ₹1,75,000 (C). Not adding back goodwill written off gives ₹2,05,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial analysis — significance to users
questions.question: Debenture holders and other long-term lenders are mainly interested in a company's:
options: A) Long-term solvency, i.e. its ability to pay interest and repay the principal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Long-term solvency, i.e. its ability to pay interest and repay the principal
Why: Long-term lenders want assurance that interest will be paid regularly and the loan repaid on maturity, so they study solvency ratios such as debt-equity and interest coverage.
Why not the others:
(B) Short-term creditors focus on daily liquidity.
(C) Market share interests management and competitors.
(D) Dividend policy interests shareholders.
Key point: Short-term creditors → liquidity; long-term lenders → solvency; shareholders → profitability.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow from operating activities — adjustments
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for a non-finance company preparing its cash flow statement by the indirect method:

List-I (Item)
(A) Depreciation
(B) Profit on sale of investments
(C) Increase in inventory
(D) Interest paid on debentures

List-II (Treatment)
(I) Deducted from net profit as a working-capital change
(II) Added back to net profit as a non-cash charge
(III) Added back to net profit and shown as an outflow under financing activities
(IV) Deducted from net profit, with the sale proceeds shown under investing activities

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why:
(A) Depreciation reduced profit without any cash outflow → add back (II).
(B) Profit on sale of investments is not operating; deduct it and show the full proceeds under investing (IV).
(C) A rise in inventory locks up cash → deduct as a working-capital change (I).
(D) Interest paid is a financing cost; add it back to profit and show the payment under financing (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the investment and inventory treatments; (B) swaps depreciation and interest; (C) swaps inventory and interest.
Key point: Non-cash items and non-operating items are removed from profit; working-capital changes are adjusted.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Preparing reports using pivot table
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about a pivot table in a spreadsheet:
(A) It can summarise data by sum, count or average.
(B) Fields can be rearranged between rows and columns to view the data differently.
(C) Changes in the source data appear in the pivot table automatically, without refreshing it.
(D) It can filter the data that is displayed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: A pivot table summarises data using functions such as sum, count and average (A), lets the user drag fields between rows and columns (B), and allows filtering (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — a pivot table is a snapshot. When the source data changes, the user must REFRESH it. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include (C).
Key point: Edit the data → refresh the pivot table.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: CAS — input documents
questions.question: In a computerised accounting system, a transaction is entered into the system through a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Voucher
Why: The voucher (receipt, payment, journal, sales or purchase voucher) is the input document. It is entered once, and the software then posts it to the ledger and generates the trial balance and financial statements.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are OUTPUTS that the system generates from the vouchers.
Key point: Input = voucher; output = ledger, trial balance, reports.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Financial functions in spreadsheet
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Function)
(A) =PMT( )
(B) =IPMT( )
(C) =PPMT( )
(D) =FV( )

List-II (Returns)
(I) Future value of an investment
(II) Interest part of a particular instalment
(III) Principal part of a particular instalment
(IV) Equal periodic instalment of a loan

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) PMT gives the equal instalment for a loan → (IV).
(B) IPMT gives the interest portion of a given instalment → (II).
(C) PPMT gives the principal portion; IPMT + PPMT = PMT → (III).
(D) FV gives the future value of regular investments → (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps IPMT and PPMT; (B) reverses PMT and FV; (C) swaps PMT and IPMT.
Key point: These functions build a loan repayment schedule — PMT for each row, split into IPMT and PPMT.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Features of CAS — security
questions.question: Which feature of a computerised accounting system ensures that a user can see or change only the data he or she is authorised to handle?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Password-based user access control
Why: CAS provides security through passwords and user rights, so that each user can access only the modules or data allotted to him. This prevents unauthorised changes and fraud.
Why not the others:
(A) Codification organises accounts.
(C) A pivot table summarises data.
(D) Automatic recalculation updates formulas.
Key point: Security in CAS = passwords + access rights + audit trail + back-up.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Payroll accounting — employer's contribution
questions.question: In payroll accounting, the employer's contribution to the Provident Fund is:
options: A) Deducted from the employee's gross salary
B) An expense of the employer, recorded in addition to the salary
C) Added to the employee's net salary paid in cash
D) Not recorded in the books
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) An expense of the employer, recorded in addition to the salary
Why: Two PF amounts arise. The EMPLOYEE's contribution is deducted from his gross salary. The EMPLOYER's matching contribution is an additional cost to the business, debited to an expense account and paid into the fund, not to the employee.
Why not the others:
(A) describes the employee's contribution.
(C) The employer's share is not paid out in cash to the employee.
(D) It is a real expense and must be recorded.
Key point: Employee PF → deduction; employer PF → expense.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan repayment schedule — total interest
questions.question: A loan of ₹2,00,000 at 8% p.a. is repaid in 2 equal annual instalments at the end of each year. The instalment (=PMT) is about ₹1,12,154. The total interest paid over the life of the loan is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹24,308
Step 1: Total paid = 2 × ₹1,12,154 = ₹2,24,308
Step 2: Total interest = ₹2,24,308 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹24,308
Check: Year 1 interest ₹16,000 (8% of ₹2,00,000), principal ₹96,154, balance ₹1,03,846; Year 2 interest ₹8,308 → total ₹24,308 ✔
Common mistake: Charging 8% on the full loan for both years gives ₹32,000 (A). ₹16,000 (B) is only the first year's interest. ₹12,154 (D) is the excess of one instalment over ₹1,00,000.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Electronic spreadsheet — ROUND function
questions.question: The value returned by =ROUND(1234.567,1) is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1234.6
Why: ROUND(number, num_digits) rounds to the given number of decimal places. With num_digits = 1, the second decimal (6) is 5 or more, so the first decimal rounds up: 1234.567 → 1234.6.
Why not the others:
(B) Truncating instead of rounding gives 1234.5.
(C) ROUND(…,0) gives 1235.
(D) ROUND(…,−1) gives 1230.
Key point: Positive digits → decimal places; zero → nearest whole number; negative → tens, hundreds and so on.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Generating accounting information — COUNTIF
questions.question: Cells C2:C7 show the payment status of six invoices: Paid, Due, Paid, Paid, Due, Paid. The value returned by =COUNTIF(C2:C7,"Paid") is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4
Why: COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts the cells in the range that meet the criteria. 'Paid' appears in C2, C4, C5 and C7.
Why not the others:
(A) 6 counts every invoice (=COUNTA).
(B) 2 counts the invoices that are Due.
(D) 1 has no basis.
Key point: COUNTIF counts; SUMIF adds the values that meet a condition.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Codification — block codes
questions.question: In a chart of accounts, the numbers 1000–1999 are reserved for assets, 2000–2999 for liabilities and 3000–3999 for capital. This method of coding is known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Block codes
Why: In block coding, a range (block) of numbers is allotted to each group of accounts, so every account within the group gets a number from that block. New accounts can be added without disturbing the structure.
Why not the others:
(B) Mnemonic codes use letters as memory aids (e.g. SAL).
(C) Sequential codes number items one after another, with no grouping.
(D) Alphabetic codes are not one of the coding methods NCERT lists.
Key point: Ranges by group → block codes.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Depreciation schedule — straight-line with salvage
questions.question: A depreciation schedule uses =SLN(50000,5000,5) for an asset costing ₹50,000 with a salvage value of ₹5,000 and a life of 5 years. The book value of the asset at the end of the third year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹23,000
Step 1: Annual depreciation = (₹50,000 − ₹5,000) ÷ 5 = ₹9,000
Step 2: Accumulated depreciation after 3 years = ₹27,000
Step 3: Book value = ₹50,000 − ₹27,000 = ₹23,000
Common mistake: Ignoring the salvage (₹10,000 a year) gives ₹20,000 (A). ₹27,000 (B) is the accumulated depreciation. Stopping after 2 years gives ₹32,000 (C).
